claims.text: Equimolar WTaTiVZr contains approximately 20 at.% each of W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr.
The WTaTiVZr HEA exhibits higher high-temperature plastic strain than commercially used pure tungsten.
The WTaTiVZr HEA exhibits higher high-temperature toughness than commercially used pure tungsten.
The higher plastic strain and toughness are primarily caused by severe lattice distortion and solid-solution strengthening arising from the multi-element composition.
W, Ta, Ti, V, and Zr are randomly distributed in the HEA.
The random multi-element distribution produces severe local lattice distortion.
The random atomic arrangement creates a complex local energy landscape.
Lattice distortion and the complex energy landscape impede dislocation motion more effectively in WTaTiVZr than in pure tungsten.
The greater impediment to dislocation motion leads to enhanced high-temperature plasticity and toughness.
At 800–1200°C, WTaTiVZr is expected to have 2–5 times the plastic strain of pure tungsten under matched testing conditions.
At 800–1200°C, WTaTiVZr is expected to have 1.5–3 times the toughness of pure tungsten under matched testing conditions.
Similar HEA systems typically show enhancements of the magnitude used for the quantitative prediction.
Pure tungsten typically has less than 1% plastic strain at high temperatures.
Pure tungsten has low high-temperature toughness because of its brittle nature.
The prediction is limited to equimolar WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten specimens with comparable grain size and density tested at 800–1200°C.
The predicted effects may not hold for non-equimolar WTaTiVZr or at much lower temperatures.
A matched tensile test at 1000°C can compare plastic strain to failure and toughness between WTaTiVZr and pure tungsten.
Failure of WTaTiVZr to reach twice the plastic strain and 1.5 times the toughness of pure tungsten at 1000°C would falsify the stated hypothesis.
